pr_title: Speed up ILEmitTrie jump table using Binary Search Tree
pr_body:
Speed up ILEmitTrie jump table using Binary Search Tree

Fixes #52812

## Description

The main change of this PR is adding Binary Search for `ILEmitTrie` instead of linear search in 3 places however a few additional optimizations were included.

1. Initially when matching the input string based on length. We use binary search to reduce the linear search to a maximum of 3 options (at which point linear search is probably faster). In cases when there are 3 or fewer different lengths, the IL hasn't changed.
2. Similarly to (1) we use binary search on the 4-character vectorized search.
    - Additionally for the vectorized search, we check if all characters we could match are ASCII letters and if so, then we can emit 14 fewer instructions (<-- kind of the same optimization as is done in [StringSearchValues](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/26722b6879f6b5f4556309e05383ecf7736870b4/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/SearchValues/Strings/Helpers/StringSearchValuesHelper.cs#L113C7-L113C7)) This helps speed up the code even if there are few too branches for binary search, and will probably result in smaller IL code size in a lot of cases.
4. We also add binary search when doing the single character. 2 further notes here as `char.ToLower` seems to be expensive to compute based on previous comments. First we compute the `character | 0x20`.
   - As we emit the comparisons, if we are comparing against a non-letter then we compare against the original character. If we compare against a letter, we compare against the `| 0x20` version.
   - The binary search is done against the `| 0x20` version of the character. This does mean that we must disable the binary search if two characters are the same after `| 0x20` is applied.

This improves the MicroBenchmarks as follows:
- VectorTrie (Count = 25, Count = 50) is now 60% of original duration. Curiously only 80% for Count = 100
- Trie (Count = 100) is now 40% of original duration. Curiously very minor / insignificant impact on other Counts

```
dotnet run -c Release --filter *JumpTableMultiple*Trie*  --launchCount 3
```

issue_context.title: Speed up ILEmitTrie jump table using Binary Search Tree
issue_context.body:
The proposal here is that we can improve `ILEmitTrie` by using binary search instead of the linear search we currently do for both finding the length as well as the vectorized search.

This improves the MicroBenchmarks as follows:
- VectorTrie (Count = 25, Count = 50) is now 60% of original duration. Curiously only 80% for Count = 100
- Trie (Count = 100) is now 40% of original duration. Curiously very minor / insignificant impact on other Counts

Implementation in https://github.com/andrewjsaid/dotnet-aspnetcore/pull/1. The PR template implied I had to first create an issue before the PR so I did so. Please let me know if design makes sense I can then point the PR to here for detailed code review.

In the linked PR you can see the changes are:
1. Binary search for length instead of linear search
2. Binary search for vectorized comparison instead of linear search
3. Where possible, binary search for single character comparison instead of linear
4. Reduce comparison of single character from 2 branches to 1
5. In vectorized comparison when only comparing letters (which is the majority of real-world cases), I removed 14 IL operations for each iteration of 4 characters. <-- kind of the same optimization as is done in [StringSearchValues](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/26722b6879f6b5f4556309e05383ecf7736870b4/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/SearchValues/Strings/Helpers/StringSearchValuesHelper.cs#L113C7-L113C7)

```
dotnet run -c Release --filter *JumpTableMultiple*Trie*  --launchCount 3
```

comments: +@javiercn @JamesNK you two are familiar with routing

I know what the ILEmitTrie does but I've never touched it. From looking at the file history, no one has made significant changes to it since @rynowak wrote it years ago. Snaps for Ryan.

If the tests all pass and perf is good then we're halfway there. I'd like to get someone to double check the vertorized path. I don't have enough expertise to review code and offer an opinion.

What should think about:
* Is the new generated IL significantly larger? There can be a lot of trie jump tables so we need to keep its size in check
* There are rules about what jump table to create. There is a check that [prefers a dictionary jump table](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/496e975d0996c5ad53e374ce3ef74840fa8555c7/src/Http/Routing/src/Matching/JumpTableBuilder.cs#L69) over a trie above 100 items. Should this change?
@andrewjsaid Go ahead and create a PR. We should have discussion in the PR.

> There are rules about what jump table to create. There is a check that [prefers a dictionary jump table](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/496e975d0996c5ad53e374ce3ef74840fa8555c7/src/Http/Routing/src/Matching/JumpTableBuilder.cs#L69) over a trie above 100 items. Should this change?

I can probably provide *some* degree of feedback on topics like this in the PR. Unfortunately it's all from memory because I didn't work on this code much after the original version 😓 

The good news is that I think the stakes probably pretty low. Most of the decisions like the switch between emit and dictionary were made empirically based on the benchmarks. So if the benchmarks change then the breakpoints should change too.

Binary search wasn't something I thought of while building the original version. Compared to the previous version of routing all of this work was in a different galaxy perf-wise 🪐 . Most of my time was spent worrying about overhead in the `N == 1` case.

> Is the new generated IL significantly larger? There can be a lot of trie jump tables so we need to keep its size in check

I think @JamesNK raises a good point about code size. Changing the complexity to `log(N)` means that the emit approach will scale to a higher breakpoint (where dictionary becomes better) than the linear version. We may not want to make this decision solely based on the throughput. In my anecdotal experience a "big" node of the routing tree has 10+ branches, not hundreds or thousands so cases that would result in big tries aren't that common.

review_comments: Might be worth mentioning how this was determined.

I arrived at this number after doing some analysis, described below. Consider that as we are emitting the code essentially "hardcoding" the tree into IL, we are able to use this heuristic to determine what is a good binary tree size.

In the table below, we analyze how the linear vs binary search tree performance varies depending on number of items, in terms of number of equality checks (`==`).
 - The BST approach implies first doing a comparison operation (`>`) to split the number of items into two buckets followed immediately by a linear search.
 - This comparison operation for BST should be kept in mind when reading the table.
 - We analyze the AverageCase scenario: number of `==` ops if all items access once, divided by number of items.
 - We analyze the WorstCase scenario: the largest number of `==` ops possible

| Items | Strategy    | AverageCase | WorstCase: |
| ----- | ----------- | ----------- | ---------- |
|     2 | Linear      |         1.5 |          2 |
|     2 | BST         |           1 |          1 |
|     3 | Linear      |           2 |          3 |
|     3 | BST         |        1.33 |          2 |
|     4 | Linear      |         2.5 |          4 |
|     4 | BST         |         1.5 |          2 |
|     5 | Linear      |           3 |          5 |
|     5 | BST         |         1.8 |          3 |

```
Working for transparency

Linear:
  2 => ( 1 + 2 ) / 2 = 1.5
  3 => ( 1 + 2 + 3 ) / 3 = 2
  4 => ( 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 ) / 4 = 2.5
  5 => ( 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 ) / 5 = 3

BST
  2 => (1 + 1) / 2 = 1
  3 => (1 + 2 + 1) / 3 = 1.33
  4 => (1 + 2 + 1 + 2) / 4 = 1.5
  5 => (1 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2) / 5 = 1.8
```


Based on the table above, and keeping in mind that the BST approach **always implies a single extra comparison/branch step**, we conclude:
1. For 2 and 3 items Linear is better in both Average and Worst Cases (when considering the extra comparison/branch)
2. For 4 items, I decided that the cost of the extra comparison/branch is worth the reduction of AverageCase from 5 -> 2 and WrostCase from 4 -> 2.
3. For 5+ items, the benefit starts to become much clearer.
Not sure if i'm reading this the wrong way, but I can't understand how the average case can be worst than the worst case for linear comparisons with values 4 and 5.

On review, it's clear to me that I've divided by 2 instead of `count`. There were a few other mistakes too which I have updated alongside my working for transparency.

I've updated the table and added my working to regain some credibility I guess 🤷
